title: Depression Applications
subtitle: Experimental regulation targets, not established first-line care
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical diagram illustrating depression applications within a neurofeedback closed loop.
tags: promising but insufficient for routine first-line use
searchTerms: promising but insufficient for routine first-line use
learningObjectives: Explain depression applications without diagnostic overreach.
Distinguish measurement, mechanism and clinical outcome in depression applications.
Identify one safety or validity limitation relevant to depression applications.

sections.explainSimply: Neurofeedback research in depression targets patterns related to mood, approach, reward or emotion regulation.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Studies vary across EEG asymmetry, source, connectivity and fMRI paradigms. Small samples and heterogeneous protocols limit conclusions.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Use validated symptom and risk monitoring, including suicidality. Neurofeedback should not delay established treatments or medical review.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Testing a treatment hypothesis: improvement must be meaningful, measured and compared with plausible alternatives.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need to understand depression applications to evaluate mechanism claims, informed consent, treatment fit and whether change transfers to real-world function.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: A changing EEG metric does not guarantee mood recovery or safety.
sections.clinicalPearl: Measure benefit and harm with the same seriousness.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using depression applications predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: A changing EEG metric does not guarantee mood recovery or safety. Evidence classification: promising but insufficient for routine first-line use.
